q: The work done by a constant force on a body is negative when the angle between the force and the displacement is:
x: W = Fd cos θ, and cos θ is negative for 90° < θ ≤ 180°, for example friction opposing motion. At 90° the work is zero; below 90° it is positive.

q: A 2 kg ball is thrown vertically upward and rises 5 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the work done on the ball by gravity during the rise is:
x: Gravity (20 N) acts downward while the displacement is 5 m upward, so W = 20 × 5 × cos 180° = −100 J. Ignoring the direction gives +100 J; using the mass instead of the weight gives −10 J.

q: A force acting along a straight line is +20 N for the first 2 m of displacement and then −10 N (opposite to the motion) for the next 2 m. The net work done by the force over the 4 m is:
x: Work = area under the force–displacement graph, counting area below the axis as negative: 20 × 2 + (−10) × 2 = 40 − 20 = 20 J. Adding both areas as positive gives 60 J; taking only the first part gives 40 J.

q: A spring of spring constant 200 N m⁻¹ is already stretched by 0.1 m. The extra work needed to stretch it slowly from an extension of 0.1 m to 0.2 m is:
x: W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²) = ½ × 200 × (0.04 − 0.01) = 3 J (the area of the trapezium under the F–x graph from 20 N to 40 N: ½(20 + 40) × 0.1 = 3 J). Using ½k(Δx)² gives 1 J; stretching from zero to 0.2 m gives 4 J.

q: A constant force F = (2î + 3ĵ) N acts on a particle while it moves from the point (1, 2) m to the point (4, 6) m. The work done by the force is:
x: Displacement d = (4 − 1)î + (6 − 2)ĵ = 3î + 4ĵ m, so W = F · d = 2 × 3 + 3 × 4 = 18 J. Using the final position vector instead of the displacement gives 26 J; multiplying the magnitudes √13 × 5 assumes F and d are parallel.

q: A force F does work on a body while it moves a distance d, the force making 60° with the displacement (cos 60° = 0.5). If instead a force 2F acts along the displacement over the same distance d, the work done becomes:
x: W₁ = Fd cos 60° = 0.5Fd and W₂ = 2Fd cos 0° = 2Fd, so W₂/W₁ = 4. Doubling the force alone, without the change from cos 60° to cos 0°, gives the tempting twice as large.

q: A constant upward force of 30 N lifts a 2 kg mass vertically through 5 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the net work done on the mass by all the forces is:
x: Work by the 30 N force = 30 × 5 = 150 J; work by gravity = −20 × 5 = −100 J; net work = 50 J, which equals the mass's gain in kinetic energy. 150 J is the work of the applied force alone.

q: A 2 kg book is lifted onto a shelf 3 m above the floor. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², its gain in gravitational potential energy is:
x: ΔPE = mgh = 2 × 10 × 3 = 60 J. Leaving out g gives 6 J; halving as if it were kinetic energy gives 30 J.

q: The kinetic energy of a body of fixed mass increases by 44 %. Its momentum increases by:
x: K = p²/2m, so p ∝ √K: √1.44 = 1.2, an increase of 20 %. Check: if p rises 20 %, K rises by 1.2² = 1.44, that is 44 %. Halving 44 % gives the tempting 22 %.

q: A 0.1 kg ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹ and, because of air resistance, rises only 15 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the energy lost to air resistance during the rise is:
x: Initial KE = ½ × 0.1 × 20² = 20 J; PE at the top = 0.1 × 10 × 15 = 15 J; energy lost = 20 − 15 = 5 J. 20 J and 15 J are the two energies themselves, not their difference.

q: A net work of 64 J is done on a 2 kg body that was initially at rest. Its final speed is:
x: By the work–energy principle, ½mv² = 64, so v² = 64 and v = 8 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the ½ (2v² = 64) gives 4√2 m s⁻¹; forgetting the square root gives 32 m s⁻¹.

q: A pendulum bob is released from rest at a point 0.8 m higher than its lowest point. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed at the lowest point is:
x: PE lost = KE gained: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √16 = 4 m s⁻¹; the mass cancels. Forgetting the square root gives 16 m s⁻¹; dropping the 2 gives √8 = 2√2 m s⁻¹.

q: A 4 kg block slides on a rough horizontal floor against a constant friction force. Its speed falls from 6 m s⁻¹ to 4 m s⁻¹ while it slides 5 m. How much farther does it slide before stopping?
x: Friction = loss of KE/distance = ½ × 4 × (36 − 16)/5 = 40/5 = 8 N; the remaining KE ½ × 4 × 16 = 32 J is removed in 32/8 = 4 m. Check: v² falls by 20 over 5 m (4 per metre), and 16 is left, so 4 m. Assuming the speed falls equally per metre gives 10 m.

q: A 1 kg ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its speed at the point where its kinetic energy equals its potential energy (measured from the ground) is:
x: Total energy = mgH = 200 J; KE = PE when each is 100 J, at a height of 10 m. Then ½ × 1 × v² = 100, so v = √200 = 10√2 m s⁻¹. 20 m s⁻¹ is its speed on reaching the ground.

q: With g the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a planet of radius R, the escape velocity from its surface is:
x: Since GM = gR², v = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR²/R) = √(2gR). √(gR) is the speed of a satellite orbiting close to the surface, which lacks the factor 2.

q: The ratio of the escape velocity from the Earth's surface to the speed of a satellite in a circular orbit just above the surface is:
x: Escape velocity = √(2gR) and orbital speed close to the surface = √(gR), so the ratio is √2. Forgetting the square root gives 2; inverting the ratio gives 1/√2.

q: A planet has the same average density as the Earth but twice the Earth's radius. If the escape velocity from the Earth is v, the escape velocity from the planet is:
x: With the same density, M ∝ R³, so M/R ∝ R² and v = √(2GM/R) ∝ R; twice the radius gives 2v. Check: mass 8 times, radius 2 times, √(8/2) = 2. Forgetting that the mass also grows gives √2 v or a smaller value.

q: The absolute gravitational potential energy of a body on the Earth's surface is −U₀. At a distance of 3R from the Earth's centre, where R is the Earth's radius, its absolute potential energy is:
x: U = −GMm/r, so U ∝ 1/r: at r = 3R it is −U₀/3. Using 1/r² as for the force gives −U₀/9; reading 3R as a height above the surface (r = 4R) gives −U₀/4.

q: Ignoring air resistance and the Earth's rotation, the escape velocity of a body launched from the Earth's surface:
o: Is least when it is launched vertically upward
Is least when it is launched horizontally
Does not depend on the direction in which it is launched
Is greatest when it is launched at 45°
x: Escape depends only on energy: ½mv² must equal GMm/R. Kinetic energy is a scalar, so the same speed is needed in any direction (as long as the path does not hit the Earth). Thinking of it like a projectile range is the slip.

q: Ignoring air resistance, a body is to be launched vertically upward from the Earth's surface so that it just reaches a height equal to the Earth's radius R. With g = 10 m s⁻² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, the launch speed needed is:
x: ½mv² = GMm/R − GMm/2R = GMm/2R = ½mgR, so v = √(gR) = √(6.4 × 10⁷) = 8 × 10³ m s⁻¹ = 8 km s⁻¹. Using mgh with h = R (constant g) gives √(2gR) = 8√2 km s⁻¹, the escape velocity, which is too large.

q: A body is launched from the Earth's surface with exactly the escape velocity. Taking absolute potential energy as zero at infinity and ignoring air resistance, the total energy (kinetic plus potential) of the body is:
x: At launch KE = ½mv² = GMm/R and PE = −GMm/R, so the total is zero, and it stays zero as the body just reaches infinity with zero speed. −GMm/2R is the total energy of a satellite in orbit at radius R, a bound state.

q: One watt is equal to:
x: Power = work/time, so 1 W = 1 J per second = 1 J s⁻¹. 1 J s is the unit of Planck's constant and 1 kg m s⁻² is the newton.

q: An electric motor takes in 500 W and lifts a 40 kg load vertically at a steady 1 m s⁻¹. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the efficiency of the motor is:
x: Useful output power = Fv = mgv = 40 × 10 × 1 = 400 W, so efficiency = 400/500 × 100 = 80 %. Inverting the ratio gives an impossible 125 %; leaving out g gives 8 %.

q: A 1000 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s on a level road. Ignoring friction and air resistance, the average power of its engine is:
x: Work done = gain in KE = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 2 × 10⁵ J; average power = 2 × 10⁵/10 = 2 × 10⁴ W = 20 kW. Forgetting the ½ gives 40 kW; not dividing by the time gives 200 kW.

q: A constant net force accelerates a body from rest along a straight line. The power delivered by the force:
o: Increases in proportion to the time
Increases in proportion to the square of the time
x: P = Fv, and with a constant force v = at grows in proportion to t, so P = Fat ∝ t. Thinking constant force means constant power is the usual error; it is the kinetic energy that grows as t².

q: A 1000 kg car climbs a straight slope that rises 1 m for every 20 m along the road (sin θ = 1/20) at a steady 10 m s⁻¹. The resistive forces total 500 N. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the power of the engine is:
x: Driving force = mg sin θ + resistance = 1000 × 10/20 + 500 = 1000 N; P = Fv = 1000 × 10 = 10 kW. Check: per second it lifts 1000 kg by 0.5 m (5 kW) and works 500 N over 10 m (5 kW). Forgetting either part gives 5 kW; using the full weight gives 105 kW.

q: A 2 kg ball is thrown vertically downward at 10 m s⁻¹ from a height of 15 m. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², its kinetic energy just before it hits the ground is:
x: By conservation of energy, KE at the ground = initial KE + PE lost = ½ × 2 × 10² + 2 × 10 × 15 = 100 + 300 = 400 J. Check: v² = 100 + 2 × 10 × 15 = 400, KE = ½ × 2 × 400 = 400 J. Forgetting the initial KE gives 300 J.
